I've completed the analysis. Here is the incident report.

---

## Incident Report — Host Compromise, DESKTOP-SKBR25F

**Evidence reviewed:** `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (11,562 frames, 585.7 sec, 2024-07-30 06:38:48 – 06:48:34 UTC+4). No separate IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence directory — findings below are derived directly from packet analysis with tshark.

### Victim host
| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | 172.16.1.66 |
| MAC address | 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08 |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-SKBR25F |
| Logged-in domain user | `ccollier` (domain `WIRESHARKWORKSHOP`, AD domain `wiresharkworkshop.online`, DC `WIRESHARK-WS-DC` at 172.16.1.4) |

Confirmed via Kerberos CNameString (`ccollier`), NTLMSSP (`DESKTOP-SKBR25F$` / domain `WIRESHARKWORKSH`), and DNS self-registration (`DESKTOP-SKBR25F.wiresharkworkshop.online`). Only this single host on the /24 exhibits infection indicators.

### Malware family
**StrRAT** — **signature-confirmed**, not just behavioral. The malware's own plaintext C2 check-in protocol contains the literal string `STRRAT` and self-reports its version:

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender||1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|<uptime>
```

- Client/campaign ID: `1BE8292C`
- Reported malware version: `1.6`
- Field `Not Installed` (AV real-time status per StrRAT's own AV-check routine) and `Windows Defender` as detected AV product, both self-reported by the malware, not independently verified against host state.
- The beacon repeats every ~5 seconds for the full remainder of the capture (first sent at T+78.07s, continuing through T+585.66s, the last frame in the file) — no operator interaction (no file transfer/keylogging/screenshot commands) is present in the captured window, only the heartbeat "ping".

### Indicators of Compromise (grounded in traffic)

**Command-and-control**
- `141.98.10.79:12132` (TCP) — StrRAT C2 endpoint. Single persistent session, `tcp.stream 83`, client port 49754. Traffic is plaintext (not TLS) length-prefixed text (`<len>\r\n\r\n<data>`).

**Supporting behavioral indicator**
- `GET http://ip-api.com/json/` to 208.95.112.1 at T+78.0s, using a spoofed `Chrome/73.0.3683.86` User-Agent (inconsistent with the Edge/WebView UAs used by this host's legitimate Microsoft traffic). Response revealed the host's public IP/geolocation (136.49.34.127, Austin, TX, Google Fiber). The result (`US:United States`) appears verbatim in the StrRAT beacon one second later, directly linking this lookup to the RAT's self-recon behavior.

**Malicious domain**
- None observed for the C2 channel itself — the C2 (141.98.10.79:12132) was contacted by raw IP, no DNS lookup preceded it in this capture.

**URLs**
- `http://ip-api.com/json/` (geolocation recon by the implant, not itself a payload-hosting URL).

**Transferred files / hashes**
- **None recoverable.** No plaintext (HTTP) file transfer of an executable, JAR, or archive occurs in this capture — the only two HTTP objects present are `msftconnecttest.txt` (benign NCSI probe) and the `ip-api.com` JSON response. Larger downloads seen in the capture (to `objects.githubusercontent.com` 185.199.110.133, `repo1.maven.org` 199.232.196.209, and `github.com` 140.82.113.3, all beginning ~T+64–68s, roughly 13 seconds before the first C2 beacon) are TLS-encrypted end to end, so no filename, content-type, or SHA256 hash can be extracted from this pcap. This timing is worth flagging as a possible delivery/staging correlation (StrRAT is Java-based and requires a JRE, consistent with GitHub/Maven fetch activity shortly before beaconing starts), but it is **not confirmed malicious** from this evidence alone — do not report a hash or filename that isn't actually observable in the traffic.

### Bottom line
DESKTOP-SKBR25F (172.16.1.66, user ccollier) is actively compromised with **StrRAT v1.6** (client ID `1BE8292C`), beaconing continuously to **141.98.10.79:12132** for the entire captured session. Recommend isolating the host, blocking 141.98.10.79/32 (and port 12132 outbound) at the perimeter, and forensic imaging of the endpoint to recover the dropper/JAR and compute hashes, since the capture alone cannot yield the payload artifact.
